slides.0.title: Pyrenean foothills: Jurançon, Béarn and Irouléguy
slides.0.subtitle: Mountains, wind and sweet whites
slides.1.title: The Jurançon rules
slides.1.highlights.0.title: AOC
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Sweet wines gained AOC in 1936 and Jurançon Sec in 1975 (Wine With Seth); Vendanges Tardives followed in 1995 (Wine With Seth Petit Manseng page)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Varieties
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Gros and Petit Manseng together at least 50%; only Petit and Gros Manseng in Vendanges Tardives; support varieties are Courbu Blanc, Petit Courbu, Camaralet de Lasseube and Lauzet (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Scale and split
slides.1.highlights.2.content: About 1,000 ha across 25 communes; dry wines about 75% and sweet about 25% (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.content: People think of Jurançon as sweet, yet dry wines are three-quarters of output.
slides.2.title: Passerillage and sweetness
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Passerillage
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Sweet wines are concentrated by drying on the vine rather than by botrytis; Petit Manseng can hang until November or December, helped by the foehn (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Sugar thresholds
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Jurançon Sec at most 4 g/L; sweet at least 40 g/L; Vendanges Tardives at least 55 g/L (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: High training
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Vines are trained up to about 2 m to reduce ground-frost risk; Jurançon has about 3,000 vines/ha versus 10,000 in Bordeaux and Burgundy (Wine With Seth)
slides.2.content: These are sweet wines shaped by dry wind, not by mould.
slides.3.title: Béarn
slides.3.highlights.0.title: History and rules
slides.3.highlights.0.content: A VDQS in 1951 and an AOC in 1975; Béarn-Bellocq created in 1991; about 259 ha (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Varieties
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Six red varieties: Cabernet Franc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Tannat, Fer, Manseng Noir and Courbu Noir; seven conservation white varieties (Wikipedia)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Rainfall
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Rainfall ranges from about 1,300 mm at Salies-de-Béarn to about 1,000 mm at Madiran; the Pyrenees block rain clouds and produce foehn winds (Wikipedia)
slides.3.content: Reds and rosés make up most of Béarn's output.
slides.4.title: Irouléguy
slides.4.highlights.0.title: History
slides.4.highlights.0.content: In the 11th century monks of the Abbey of Roncesvalles planted the first large vineyards to supply pilgrims on the Way of St James; after the Treaty of the Pyrenees in 1659 villagers took over (Wikipedia)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: Terraces
slides.4.highlights.1.content: Vineyards sit on terraces at 100–400 m, with some slopes reaching 60°; the soils are deep red (Wikipedia)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: Scale
slides.4.highlights.2.content: AOC in October 1970; about 500 ha in the 17th century, only about 70 ha in the 1980s and about 210 ha today; output is roughly 70% red, 20% rosé and 10% white (Wikipedia)
slides.4.content: Irouléguy is the only AOP of the Basque area, per Wine Folly.
